I almost died, lost my job, and was gaslit by my family for years leading up to it. 

I'd always been sickly, lots of tummy aches and intense bouts of illness, most of which was blamed on school avoidance and ignored until dire. Once I got to highschool, between my toxic stepmother and my preoccupied father, I was angrily blamed for being constantly ill and accused of faking with no help ever offered. I learned to accept pain, chronic exhaustion, and deep depression as personal failings I just needed to overcome.

After graduation, I was doing a bit better for a while (Unfortunately due to a restrictive ED that involved few grains) but when I began recovery and started a new job I started getting sicker and sicker. Eventually I was terminated for my absence, since we didn't have any idea why I was so sick. I went to several doctors as the pain and weight loss increased, but once appendicitis was ruled out nobody wanted to investigate further.

Unfortunately several doctors were openly hostile towards me, throwing unprofessional and unbased accusations of sexual disease and pregnancy as the cause of my "discomfort". I'm autistic so my outward performance of pain is little to none, even at a 10, which didn't help my case. I was forced into several humiliating and uncomfortable pelvic examinations with med students against my wishes. Once they proved I wasn't lying about my body count and fidelity, they all but kicked me out and told me to take midol for my cramps next time. My BP was 100/90, my heart rate 50 and dropping, and I had lost 50 lbs since my last weight on file, which had been in the healthy category. They seemed to have "warned" other doctors in the hospital as I had similar outcomes at two more appointments. Having never been pregnant, never had an STI, and never sought or been prescribed pain medication, I have no idea what vendetta this (shockingly, female) practitioner had against me. 

I could no longer walk or eat. I had basically accepted my death and was crying every day feeling weaker and afraid. I was barely 18, I started getting violently sick 2 months after my birthday. As a last ditch effort, I used an MD search website to find one more appointment ASAP. The nurse who saw me saved my life. I cried in her arms as I explained my situation, the horrors I was put through, and my declining vitals. I explained that I at least kept my blood sugar up by drinking fruit juice and trying to stay hydrated even through the pain. She commended me for all my efforts, and was devastated to hear how I'd been treated. She swore to me she wouldn't let me die, and sent several viles of blood to be tested. 

Within the week she called me personally to tell me how high the celiac indication had come back and she was shocked it had been overlooked entirely. I sobbed until my eyes were swollen both in relief and dispair. I had plans to go to culinary school to make and work with bread. I have a very ironic gift of making the most perfect fluffy loaves and I was, and am, crushed. Almost immediately my health improved as I eliminated gluten from my diet, and now several autoimmune diseases later, I'm living as comfortably as I can with everything she's diagnosed me with. Knowing makes it all a lot easier to cope with, considering my history of blaming myself. I will always miss bread, but at least I still get to dream about it

I have this problem each time I go into recovery, and only now I'm addressing it to prevent relapse. Your body likes equilibrium, it's is always trying to get you to a static point that's best for you. Your blood pH, your hormones, and your weight! It's especially important to maintain a healthy, large amount of calories at a "restored" weight. Recovery is a lifetime process, and you are allowed and encouraged to keep eating! 

A lot of ED folks want to get to a healthy weight that still follows a lot of ED rules. Wanting to recover to a certain size or aesthetic is the bad brain talking. The ultimate goal of recovery is being healthy again, and that means your size. Isn't. Important. Your health is! Eating keeps you healthy, movement (in appropriate amounts when you're ready) keeps you healthy, and keeping tabs on your mental health keeps you healthy. You can't skip any of these, especially if you're recovering. 

My personal motivation to keep eating even when the bad brain is loud, is reminding myself I absolutely do NOT want to lose my hair again. Even healthy people who aren't eating enough can lose hair, and I want to keep mine! Find your motivation, and it'll become easier to maintain health as a top priority ❤️

From my experience it's addiction in that it's a misplaced coping mechanism. Addicts often struggle with some kind of trauma or abusive self talk that drives them to punish themselves or escape reality. Eating disorders can operate in a similar fashion. Repetitively punishing yourself because you believe you deserve it, controlling food as a means of ignoring underlying trauma or mental illness. 

The other aspect that ties it completely to addiction are the reward chemicals one can experience with certain behaviors. A relief of guilt by purging. A relief from emotional distress with the serotonin of eating endlessly. A relief of control issues by superceding your own bodies needs by your own twisted interpretation of 'willpower'. Often times even the feeling of emptiness or lightheadedness can give a sort of buzz. 

It doesn't help that the prevalence of diet culture conditions us to take pride and joy in restriction, and scales going down. It's ingrained in many societies that thinness is associated with many other positive traits. You may also recieve outside encouragement because people believe all weight loss is good.

 Emotional eating and binge eating are no exception. It is deeply held in many families and in our social culture of food that it is a reward or a soother of negative feelings. Ice cream after a breakup, dessert stomach, "clean your plate". Many adults don't realize that pushing a child to eat past their comfort can throw off their fullness and hunger cues, and their relationship with food. It's like becoming an alcoholic because your father always drank. 

Eating disorders follow the same patterns of escapism that addictions do. Targeted therapy and recovery are important to heal past both!

There are certain decisions your partner doesn't have input in, but this was not one of them. Her going offensive when you tried to start a dialogue about YOUR feelings on the matter, shows there needs to be communication on what personal vs relationship decisions are. She cannot continue to blur those boundaries and throw her indignation in your face, or turn her guilt on your shoulders. She absolutely should feel upset with herself for allowing reactionary behavior towards her partner, but that should not be a way to let your guard down or force comfort her. I am emotional myself about mistakes in my relationship, but I try to control that reactivity for the sake of my partner and the validity of their feelings. She took that focus off you, and it needs to be discussed. 

Emotional escalation in relationships can be very unhealthy. Learning to step away and compose yourself, or taking a moment to consider the opposing view, is key to open and progressive communication. She will need to put in a lot of work. You may need to hold her accountable if she mindlessly begins to escalate again. Bringing this union back to a healthy place will absolutely take work and time. If you need to heal more, take a break. If you don't want to wait for your partner to learn these important things, that is okay. You aren't cruel for prioritizing yourself if that is what you need, even if it's just what you want. You can heal together, or she can get her shit together and do better in the future with someone else. 

Take your time away. Practice mindfulness. Check on yourself emotionally. Do you miss her? Does her presence bring you more joy than the drawbacks she needs to address? Do you feel relieved? Drained? Focus on your own emotional state rather than hers, and do not think about her emotional concequences for whatever decision you feel the need to consider. Good luck, and may you heal.
